voice: Grand, entitled, vain, criminally self-assured, and increasingly panicked; theatrical emphasis comes from diction and rhythm rather than incessant typographic shouting.

entries.text: Well, well. Good evening, Countess.
What are you doing here?
I happened to be hiding behind the tapestry.
You're lying.
How could you tell?
No one simply happens to hide behind a museum tapestry.
And no one simply strolls through a museum after hours with paintings under her arms.
Paintings? Oh, these? I found them lying on the floor and picked them up before someone stepped on them.
I don't believe you.
Are you accusing me of something, you impertinent girl?
What do you think?
I think you are a rude young woman in desperate need of manners. The nerve, accusing people of stealing paintings!
Did I say anything about stealing them?
Of course you did. Do not play games with me, girl. I have more tricks than you have brain cells.
Then why bring those paintings to a meeting with Dr. Carrington at this hour?
How did you know I was meeting Dr. Carrington?
I found a note beside his body.
His body? You speak as though he were dead.
He is. Dead as a doornail. You didn't know?
Another trick. Dr. Carrington is alive and well in his office.
He is certainly in his office, but he is quite dead.
Good God.
Which makes you a rather obvious suspect.
Now see here! You will not pin this on me. I had no reason to kill him--we had a perfectly profitable art-burglary arrangement!
Art burglary?
I may have said too much.
If you're trying to appear innocent, you're doing a poor job of it.
Why should I care what you think? You are not a police officer.
But I am a reporter. I could put your name in the newspaper, ruin your reputation, and interest the police. But you're tough; I'm sure you could manage.
It was a modest arrangement with Dr. Carrington. A forger copied the paintings, we hung the copies in place of the originals, and sold the originals to private collectors.
Didn't you think someone would notice?

That was the beauty of it. Once every painting had been replaced, we would slash the forgeries and make it appear the originals had been vandalized. No one would suspect anyone had commissioned forgeries merely to destroy them.
Carrington made certain no one became too curious.
You mean he did.
I had nothing to do with his death! He was my cash cow. I brought him from Europe for this very purpose. That is all I shall say.
I found an interesting diary in Carrington's wall safe. It belonged to Sterling Waldorf-Carlton, your former husband.
Sterling's diary? What did you do with it?
I left it in the safe for the police.
You did not read it, I hope.
I did. It had some interesting things to say about you.
Lies, all of it. I loved Sterling. I still do, despite that business with his will. He made me a wealthy woman--or will, once the estate is settled.
Sterling believed you wanted to kill him for his money.
Lies and nonsense.
Apparently Yvette is afraid of you as well. Sterling mentioned her.
Yvette? That little trollop? So she was the woman he saw behind my back. She must have persuaded him to change his will.
I only know what I read in the diary.
Oh... I feel faint.
Perhaps you should lie down and compose yourself. We'll speak later.
Yes. A sensible suggestion.
And don't try to leave the museum. Detective O'Riley will be interested in what I know.
I am certain he will, girl. Do not worry; you and I shall speak again.
I do not care to discuss that now.
Does this look familiar?
It appears to be a pocket watch.
You'd never guess where I found it.
In your purse?
In a trunk with a human skeleton. The engraving inside says it belongs to Dr. Archibald Carrington III.
Dr. Carri--what are you saying?
Having trouble talking?
I did not kill him. Watney did.
Tell me about it.
I hired Watney to impersonate Carrington. Watney killed Carrington aboard the ship from England.
You hired him to kill Dr. Carrington?
No. That was his idea.
Then if Carrington's skeleton is in the trunk, whose body is on the desk in his office?
Then... Good God. That is Watney Little. Someone killed Watney.
Someone who believed he was the real Carrington?
How would I know? I was not there.
Who else had reason to kill him?
I don't know. Perhaps someone learned his identity, or he angered somebody. Perhaps he killed himself.
I doubt he committed suicide by impaling himself on a porcupine.
I don't know who did it. I only know it was not me. You must believe me.
Hmm.
You're not looking well, Countess.
There is a murderer loose in this museum. Naturally I am unsettled when someone leaps at me from behind an exhibit.
